title: Crostata di Marmellata
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Italy's classic jam tart, a buttery shortcrust pastry filled generously with fruit preserve and topped with a simple lattice, a homely dessert found in nearly every Italian household.
longDesc: Crostata is often the very first dessert Italian children learn to bake alongside a parent or grandparent, its forgiving pastry and simple lattice top making it an accessible, endlessly adaptable classic depending on whatever jam is on hand.
ingredients: 150 g (⅔ cup) cold unsalted butter, cubed
350 g (1¼ cups) fruit jam or preserve (such as apricot or sour cherry)
steps: Combine the flour, cold butter, sugar, and salt, working quickly with your fingertips or a pastry cutter until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.
Add the egg yolks and lemon zest, bringing the dough together quickly without overworking it.
Shape into a disc, wrap, and rest in the refrigerator for 30 minutes.
Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Roll out two-thirds of the dough and line a tart pan, trimming the edges.
Spread the jam evenly over the base.
Roll out the remaining dough and cut into strips, arranging them in a lattice pattern over the jam.
Brush the lattice lightly with beaten egg.
Bake for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is golden.
chefTips: Keep the butter cold and handle the dough as little as possible for the most tender, flaky pastry.
A good-quality, not overly sweet jam works best, as the pastry itself is already sweetened.
This is a wonderfully forgiving dessert — an uneven lattice is entirely part of its homely charm.
commonMistakes: Overworking the pastry dough, which develops gluten and results in a tough rather than tender crust.
Using a very runny jam, which can make the tart difficult to slice cleanly.
Slicing before the tart has fully cooled, when the jam filling is still too soft.
storage: Store covered at room temperature for up to 4 days.
reheating: Not applicable; served at room temperature.
healthBenefits: A source of protein from the eggs, best enjoyed as an occasional homely treat.
culturalNote: Crostata di marmellata is often the first dessert Italian children learn to bake, a simple, endlessly adaptable classic found in nearly every household across the country.
